labels.text: THEY STOOD · THEY DID NOT SING

scenes.vo: In nineteen eighty-five, three schoolchildren stood up respectfully every morning when the national anthem played. But they did not sing, because their faith did not allow it. The school expelled them.
scenes.visual: A school assembly at dawn: rows of generic children standing; three stand still with closed lips; the school gate shuts.

spec.title: Can a school make you sing?

scenes.vo: Their case reached the Supreme Court. Can a school make you sing?
scenes.visual: Title card.

scenes.vo: Hold that question. There is a bigger one in this last part.
scenes.visual: The three-stop path, the third stop lit.

labels.text: PART III · rights a court enforces
PART IV · goals no court enforces

scenes.vo: Part Three of the Constitution gives rights you can take to court. Part Four lists goals for the State that no court can enforce. So when a right and a goal collide, which one wins?
scenes.visual: Two books on a desk: PART III with a gavel, PART IV with a compass; they slide towards each other.

scenes.vo: Start with religion. Article twenty-five gives every person freedom of conscience. It also gives the right to profess, practise and propagate religion. That means to declare it, follow it and spread it. This right is for all persons, not only citizens.
scenes.visual: A notebook page: PROFESS, PRACTISE, PROPAGATE, each with a small icon; generic people of many kinds below.

labels.text: NCERT: sati, bigamy, human sacrifice may be stopped
NCERT: spreading is allowed · forcing a conversion is not

scenes.vo: But this freedom has limits written into it. It is subject to public order, morality and health. The State may also regulate economic, financial, political or other worldly activity linked to religious practice. It may pass laws for social welfare and reform. NCERT gives sati, bigamy and human sacrifice as practices the State may stop. And NCERT says spreading your faith is allowed, but forcing anyone to convert is not.
scenes.visual: The three verbs inside a frame whose edges read PUBLIC ORDER, MORALITY, HEALTH; a gear SECULAR ACTIVITY turns at the side.

labels.text: no law makes anyone sing the anthem

scenes.vo: So back to the anthem. The children had stood in respect. They had disturbed no one. The Supreme Court held that expelling them broke two rights. Freedom of speech and expression under Article nineteen, and freedom of religion under Article twenty-five. As the Court put it, no law makes anyone sing the anthem.
scenes.visual: The school gate reopens; the three children walk back in.

labels.text: own institutions · own religious affairs · property

scenes.vo: Article twenty-six is for groups. Every religious denomination may set up its own institutions and manage its own religious affairs. It may own property and run it as the law allows. In nineteen fifty-seven, this clashed with a law opening public temples to all Hindus. The Court harmonised the two. The temple had to open to the Hindu public. The denomination kept some of its own rites.
scenes.visual: A generic temple building with open doors, many people walking in; a small reserved inner space for the denomination's own rites.

labels.text: ART. 27 · no tax for one religion
ART. 28(1) · no religious instruction in wholly State-funded schools
NCERT: India has no official religion

scenes.vo: Two more rules keep the State neutral. No one can be made to pay a tax spent on promoting one particular religion. And a school wholly maintained from State funds cannot give religious instruction. The word secular was added to the Preamble by the nineteen seventy-six amendment, in force from January nineteen seventy-seven. NCERT, writing on equal treatment of all religions, says it plainly. India has no official religion.
scenes.visual: A tax receipt with a blank religion line; a State school notice ALL WELCOME; the Preamble page with SECULAR written in.

scenes.vo: Now culture and education. Article twenty-nine says any section of citizens with its own language, script or culture may conserve it. Notice the words, any section. So the text itself does not limit it to minorities, though the article's heading speaks of them. And no State-run or State-aided school may refuse a citizen only for religion, race, caste or language.
scenes.visual: Many scripts on a long ribbon across the screen, generic and varied; a school door with an open sign.

labels.text: schools and colleges of their choice

scenes.vo: Article thirty goes further for minorities. Religious and linguistic minorities may set up and run schools and colleges of their choice. The State cannot refuse aid to a school just because a minority manages it. Yet the Constitution never defines who counts as a minority. NCERT describes a group outnumbered in a part of the country or the whole.
scenes.visual: A plain school with a nameplate MANAGED BY A MINORITY; an aid envelope reaches it like any other school; a dictionary page MINORITY, its definition blank.

lines.text: NCERT Class 8: some people feel minority protections may go against secularism
Art. 29: no denial of admission on religion, race, caste or language
Art. 30: minorities may run their own institutions

scenes.vo: But NCERT itself notes a debate. NCERT Class Eight says the two aims can seem to clash. It says some people feel minority protections may go against secularism. Here is our reading of the text. Article twenty-nine bars denial of admission on religion, race, caste or language. Article thirty lets minorities run their own institutions. Both are in the Constitution.
scenes.visual: Two equal speech bubbles with no faces, then the Article 29 and 30 cards; neutral.

labels.text: ARTICLE 32 · going to the Supreme Court is a right
Ambedkar, 9 Dec 1948: 'the very soul … the very heart'

scenes.vo: A right is only as strong as the way to enforce it. So Article thirty-two makes going to the Supreme Court a right in itself. The Court can issue orders and writs to enforce your rights. Under Article two hundred twenty-six, every High Court can too. Ambedkar told the Constituent Assembly it was the very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it.
scenes.visual: A courthouse door ART. 32 with a key turning in it; a smaller door ART. 226; a faceless silhouette at a lectern with a name plaque.

labels.text: opened in the basic structure episode

scenes.vo: But Part Three has its own outer limits. Parliament decides how far these rights apply to the armed forces. It can also protect acts done to restore order where martial law was in force. And some land and policy laws are shielded from challenge on some of these rights. Laws in the Ninth Schedule, as the text reads, on all of them. We will open that box in the basic structure episode.
scenes.visual: The rights shelf with a fence at its edge ARTS 33-34, and a sealed box NINTH SCHEDULE set aside with a tag.

labels.text: GOALS, not rights to sue for

scenes.vo: But rights are not the whole book. Now Part Four, the Directive Principles. Article thirty-seven says no court can enforce them. Yet it calls them fundamental in the governance of the country. The State has a duty to apply them when it makes laws. So they are not rights you can sue for. They are goals the State has promised to work towards.
scenes.visual: The PART IV book opens into a compass; its needle points to a horizon marked GOALS. No gavel on this side.

labels.text: 45 · care for every child below six

scenes.vo: The goals are broad. A livelihood for men and women, and equal pay for equal work. Resources shared for the common good. Village panchayats with the powers to govern themselves. The right to work and to public help in old age, sickness and unemployment, within the State's means. A living wage. Care and education for every child below six. Judges kept separate from the executive in the State's public services. And a uniform civil code, and better nutrition and public health.
scenes.visual: A horizon of signposts, one per goal with its article number, appearing as each is named; text only for Article 44.

labels.text: NCERT: zamindari laws opposed as violating property
PROPERTY · a Part III right until June 1979
ART. 300A · only by authority of law

scenes.vo: But these goals ran into rights. NCERT says laws to abolish the zamindari system were opposed as violating the right to property. A long legal battle followed. NCERT says the court held that Fundamental Rights were so sacred they could not be limited even for these goals. Property itself was a fundamental right until June nineteen seventy-nine. Since then it is no longer a fundamental right. Article three hundred A, in another part of the Constitution, protects it. The State can take your property only by authority of law.
scenes.visual: The two books collide; a land map between them tears; a card PROPERTY moves from the PART III shelf to a plinth ART. 300A.

labels.text: MINERVA MILLS (1980): the balance is a basic feature

scenes.vo: So which one wins? Neither wins outright. The Minerva Mills case was decided in nineteen eighty. The majority held that the balance between Part Three and Part Four is itself a basic feature. Neither can be given absolute primacy over the other.
scenes.visual: The brass balance, PART III and PART IV level.

lines.text: Property Owners Association (2024), nine judges: Article 31C as upheld in Kesavananda stands
the wider version of 1976: struck down in Minerva Mills

scenes.vo: In twenty twenty-four, nine judges held that Article thirty-one C, as the Kesavananda Bharati case upheld it, still stands. The wider version from nineteen seventy-six had been struck down in Minerva Mills.
scenes.visual: Citation card.

lines.text: the eleventh: a child of six to fourteen gets to study
rights do not wait for duties (NCERT)

scenes.vo: Rights also come with duties. Article fifty-one A lists eleven Fundamental Duties. Ten came with the nineteen seventy-six amendment, in force from January nineteen seventy-seven. The eleventh was added later. Parents and guardians must give a child aged six to fourteen the chance to study. No clause lets a court enforce these duties. And NCERT says your rights do not depend on doing them first.
scenes.visual: The girl's notebook: a page of duties; a school bag beside the eleventh.

scenes.vo: And when a public servant violates human rights, the National Human Rights Commission can step in. It was set up under the Protection of Human Rights Act, nineteen ninety-three. It can inquire and recommend. It cannot punish anyone itself.
scenes.visual: A plain office door; a recommendation letter goes out; no gavel.

labels.text: NEITHER SIMPLY WINS · the balance is a basic feature

scenes.vo: So, rights you can enforce, and goals you cannot. When they clash, neither simply wins. The Supreme Court has held that the balance between them is a basic feature.
scenes.visual: The balance stays level.

lines.text: Arts 25-28: religion, within order, morality, health
Art. 32: the remedy is a right · Part IV guides, not enforced
Minerva Mills: the balance · Art. 300A · eleven duties

scenes.vo: For the exam, write it this way. Articles twenty-five to twenty-eight give freedom of religion, within public order, morality and health. Articles twenty-nine and thirty protect culture and minority education. Article thirty-two makes the remedy a right. The Directive Principles guide the State but cannot be enforced. In Minerva Mills the majority held their balance with rights a basic feature. Property is no longer a fundamental right; Article three hundred A protects it. And there are eleven duties.
scenes.visual: The girl's notebook: the old question struck out; the exam lines fill in.

labels.text: PART 3 · done · NEXT: the five writs

scenes.vo: That completes Fundamental Rights. Next, the five writs that Article thirty-two promised, one by one.
scenes.visual: The three-stop path, all stops lit; a road sign ahead: THE FIVE WRITS.
